Terminology

Source: vignettes/terminology.Rmd
terminology.Rmd
library(rray)

Introduction

Words like “dimension” and “size” get used loosely when talking about arrays. rray gives each of them one precise meaning, and uses that meaning everywhere, from function names to argument names to error messages. This vignette defines each term.

We’ll use this array for most examples:

x <- array(1:12, dim = c(2, 3, 2))
x
#> , , 1
#> 
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    3    5
#> [2,]    2    4    6
#> 
#> , , 2
#> 
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    7    9   11
#> [2,]    8   10   12

Axis

An axis is a single integer that picks a direction along the array. Axis 1 runs down the rows, axis 2 runs across the columns, and so on.

Many rray functions work “along an axis”. Summing along axis 1 adds up the rows, so only 1 row is left:

rray_sum(x, axes = 1)
#> , , 1
#> 
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    3    7   11
#> 
#> , , 2
#> 
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]   15   19   23

Summing along axis 3 conceptually adds the two matrices embedded in x together, so only one is left:

rray_sum(x, axes = 3)
#> , , 1
#> 
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    8   12   16
#> [2,]   10   14   18

Notice that only the axis you pick changes. Every other axis keeps its original shape.

You can also provide an axis by its title rather than its position. See ?faq-axes for more.

Dimension

A dimension is the number of elements along one axis. For x:

  • Axis 1 has a dimension of 2.

  • Axis 2 has a dimension of 3.

  • Axis 3 has a dimension of 2.

To get the dimension of one axis, index into the dimensions:

axis <- 2
rray_dimensions(x)[[axis]]
#> [1] 3

Dimensions

The dimensions are an integer vector holding the dimension of every axis.

rray_dimensions(x)
#> [1] 2 3 2

This is like dim(), except that it also works on plain vectors, which act like 1-D arrays:

dim(1:5)
#> NULL

rray_dimensions(1:5)
#> [1] 5

In the other vignettes, dimensions are often written out in parentheses, like (2, 3, 2) for x.

You can change the dimensions of an array with rray_set_dimensions(), as long as the total number of elements stays the same:

rray_set_dimensions(1:6, c(2, 3))
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    3    5
#> [2,]    2    4    6

Dimensionality

The dimensionality of an array is the length of the dimensions vector. This also corresponds with the number of axes it has.

rray_dimensions(x)
#> [1] 2 3 2

rray_dimensionality(x)
#> [1] 3

A vector has a dimensionality of 1, and a matrix has a dimensionality of 2:

rray_dimensionality(1:5)
#> [1] 1

rray_dimensionality(matrix(1:6, nrow = 2))
#> [1] 2

The terms so far have been carefully chosen so that programming with these concepts lends itself to object names that feel natural, like this:

dimensions <- rray_dimensions(x)
dimensionality <- rray_dimensionality(x)
axes <- seq_len(dimensionality)

for (axis in axes) {
  dimension <- dimensions[[axis]]
  print(dimension)
}
#> [1] 2
#> [1] 3
#> [1] 2

Size

The size is the total number of elements in the array. It is the product of the dimensions:

rray_dimensions(x)
#> [1] 2 3 2

2 * 3 * 2
#> [1] 12

rray_size(x)
#> [1] 12

For an array, this is the same as length(x):

length(x)
#> [1] 12

Be careful not to mix up size and dimension. Axis 2 of x has a dimension of 3, but x has a size of 12.

Names

The names are a list with one element per axis. Each element is either a character vector naming the elements along that axis, or NULL. This is the same as dimnames().

y <- rray_set_names(
  x,
  list(
    c("a", "b"),
    c("c", "d", "e"),
    c("f", "g")
  )
)
y
#> , , f
#> 
#>   c d e
#> a 1 3 5
#> b 2 4 6
#> 
#> , , g
#> 
#>   c  d  e
#> a 7  9 11
#> b 8 10 12

rray_names(y)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "a" "b"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "c" "d" "e"
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] "f" "g"

To get the names along one axis, use rray_axis_names():

rray_axis_names(y, axis = 3)
#> [1] "f" "g"

The first two axes are common enough to get their own helpers:

rray_row_names(y)
#> [1] "a" "b"

rray_column_names(y)
#> [1] "c" "d" "e"

An array without any names has NULL names:

rray_names(x)
#> NULL

Titles

The titles are the names on the list of names. There is one title per axis, and they show up when the array is printed.

z <- rray_set_titles(y, c("row", "col", "page"))
z
#> , , page = f
#> 
#>    col
#> row c d e
#>   a 1 3 5
#>   b 2 4 6
#> 
#> , , page = g
#> 
#>    col
#> row c  d  e
#>   a 7  9 11
#>   b 8 10 12

rray_titles(z)
#> [1] "row"  "col"  "page"

Titles are useful because you can refer to an axis by its title rather than its position:

rray_sum(z, axes = "col")
#> , , page = f
#> 
#>    col
#> row [,1]
#>   a    9
#>   b   12
#> 
#> , , page = g
#> 
#>    col
#> row [,1]
#>   a   27
#>   b   30

Broadcasting

Broadcasting is how rray works with inputs that have different dimensions. Axes with a dimension of 1 are repeated to match the other inputs. Here, b has 1 column, so it is repeated to match the 2 columns of a:

a <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3)
a
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    4
#> [2,]    2    5
#> [3,]    3    6

b <- matrix(c(10L, 20L, 30L))
b
#>      [,1]
#> [1,]   10
#> [2,]   20
#> [3,]   30

rray_add(a, b)
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]   11   14
#> [2,]   22   25
#> [3,]   33   36

Broadcasting is important enough to get its own vignette. See vignette("broadcasting") to learn more.
